metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
The structural floor, not the power feed, is often what stops an AI retrofit first: liquid-cooled racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries weigh far more than the enterprise racks buildings were engineered for.

The pattern is a mismatch between what a building was designed to carry and what AI hardware now weighs. Floor loading is measured as structural weight per square foot against the actual weight of installed racks, which makes it a comparison rather than a fixed ceiling. The note attached to this metric says retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected, which inverts the usual assumption that power is the hard constraint on converting existing space.

That matters for AI specifically because the weight comes from the cooling and power equipment the compute requires, not from the compute alone. Coolant, manifolds, and batteries are additions that follow from high-density racks, so the denser the workload, the more the building's slab and raised floor become the gate. A site can have power contracted and still be unable to host the racks.

What this does not tell the reader is how much weight any particular floor can take, what threshold separates a feasible retrofit from an infeasible one, or how many buildings fail. It gives the metric and the direction of the problem, not the distribution. The two related measures listed alongside it, server utilization rate and stranded power and space per cabinet, cover the electrical and space side of the same capacity question, and this metric covers only the structural one.
